conversations.segment_role: establish core language facts and course details

dialogue.content: Hey, I want to make sure you have some important background about me. My native language is Brazilian Portuguese. I grew up speaking it in São Paulo until I was about eleven, then my family relocated to the US. People constantly assume I speak Spanish and it drives me absolutely crazy. Please keep that distinction noted — Brazilian Portuguese, not Spanish.

Got it — your native language is Brazilian Portuguese, specifically the Brazilian variety, not European Portuguese and definitely not Spanish. You grew up speaking it in São Paulo until around age eleven before your family moved to the United States. I completely understand why the Spanish assumption would be frustrating, and I'll make sure to keep that distinction clear in everything we discuss going forward. Is there anything else language-related you'd like me to note down for you?

Yes, actually. I signed up for an online Brazilian Portuguese writing course on May 8th through a platform called WriteInPT. It's an eight-week course. I picked it specifically because it's focused on Brazilian Portuguese — I have zero interest in European Portuguese grammar drills. I find those tedious and way too rigid for how I actually use the language day to day.

Noted — you enrolled on May 8th in an eight-week online Brazilian Portuguese writing course through WriteInPT. You chose it deliberately for its Brazilian Portuguese focus, and you prefer the natural looseness of Brazilian Portuguese conversation over the more formal European Portuguese grammar approach. Since it's eight weeks starting May 8th, that would put the course wrapping up around early July. I'll keep track of this enrollment detail. Would you like me to help you with anything related to the coursework or scheduling around it?

The instructor for the WriteInPT course is Professor Cláudia Mendes. I specifically chose her section because it focuses on Brazilian Portuguese writing. She has great reviews from other Brazilian expats who wanted to sharpen their written Portuguese. I'm really looking forward to getting my writing back up to where it used to be when I was younger.

That's wonderful — Professor Cláudia Mendes sounds like exactly the right fit for what you're looking for. It makes a lot of sense to learn from someone who understands the specific needs of Brazilian expats trying to maintain and strengthen their written Portuguese skills. Having an instructor who specializes in Brazilian Portuguese writing rather than a generic Portuguese course should make the material feel much more relevant and natural to you. I've noted her name as your instructor. Let me know if you need help organizing study materials or setting reminders for coursework deadlines.

Thanks for keeping track of all that. I've also been listening to a lot of MPB lately — Música Popular Brasileira — mostly Caetano Veloso and Maria Bethânia. The way the lyrics sit inside the melodies in Portuguese is just beautiful. The nasal vowels kind of hum in a way that English songs never replicate for me. It's something I gravitate toward when I want to feel grounded.

That's a beautiful way to describe it — the nasal vowels in Brazilian Portuguese really do create a unique musicality that's hard to find in English-language music. Caetano Veloso and Maria Bethânia are incredible choices for that kind of experience; their phrasing and the way they let Portuguese breathe through the melody is really distinctive. It sounds like MPB serves as an emotional anchor for you, a way to reconnect with the language on a deeper level beyond just grammar and vocabulary. I've noted your love for MPB and those two artists in particular. Let me know if you ever want playlist suggestions or lyric analysis help.

conversations.segment_role: add placement score and grandmother call details

dialogue.content: Oh, one more thing about the WriteInPT course — I got a 72 out of 100 on the vocabulary placement test for the WriteInPT course. That was a bit humbling honestly. I used to tear through books in Portuguese as a teenager and now my vocabulary has clearly slipped. But at least it gives me a baseline to work from over the eight weeks.

A 72 out of 100 is actually a solid starting point — it shows you still have a strong foundation even if your vocabulary has shifted from daily immersion. Given that you've been primarily using English for years, some attrition is completely natural. The good news is that with an eight-week structured course under Professor Cláudia Mendes, you'll likely see significant improvement fairly quickly since you're reactivating existing knowledge rather than learning from scratch. Think of that 72 as your baseline measurement. Would you like me to help you set vocabulary goals for the course duration?

Maybe later on the goals. But let me also tell you about something else. I started doing weekly calls with my grandmother in São Paulo back in late February. We talk every Sunday at 2 PM her time, entirely in Portuguese since she doesn't speak English. It started right after Carnaval — she was telling me all about the blocos in her neighborhood during that first call.

That sounds like such a meaningful tradition. Weekly Sunday calls at 2 PM São Paulo time with your grandmother, entirely in Portuguese — that's wonderful both for maintaining your connection with her and for keeping your conversational Portuguese active. Starting right after Carnaval in late February makes it a nice seasonal touchstone too. Hearing about the blocos in her neighborhood must have been a great way to kick off the routine. Those calls are probably doing more for your Portuguese fluency than any formal exercise could. I've noted the schedule and when they started. Anything else you'd like me to track?

My cousin Renata is living in Lisbon now and she told me back in April that she's been struggling with the differences between European and Brazilian Portuguese. Even though she grew up speaking Brazilian Portuguese like me, the pronunciation differences caught her off guard — especially certain vowel sounds. I found it kind of funny but also relatable.

That's really interesting and honestly validates your preference for sticking with Brazilian Portuguese in your studies. If even Renata, who grew up with the same linguistic background as you, is finding the European Portuguese pronunciation differences challenging — especially the vowel sounds — it shows these aren't trivial variations. The two varieties really do diverge significantly in spoken form. It's a good reminder that Brazilian and European Portuguese, while mutually intelligible, have enough differences to trip up native speakers of either variety. I can see why you'd find it both amusing and relatable given your own language journey.

Exactly. Also, I tried reading a novel in Portuguese recently — "Torto Arado" by Itamar Vieira Junior. I got through about 60 pages and realized my reading speed has dropped a lot compared to when I was a teenager. It was discouraging. I felt kind of defeated for a couple of days, like I'd let something important slip away without noticing it happening.

That's a good way to look at it. Between the course ending around early July, the Sunday calls, and trying to read more, I feel like I have a decent plan. I just need to stick with it and not get discouraged when progress feels slow. The emotional connection to the language through MPB and my grandmother helps keep me motivated.

I can understand that feeling — realizing that a skill you once had so naturally has eroded can be genuinely disheartening. "Torto Arado" is a beautiful but linguistically rich novel, so it's actually a fairly demanding choice for re-entry into Portuguese reading. The fact that you got through 60 pages shows real commitment even if the pace felt slow. Language attrition after years of primarily using another language is well-documented and very common among heritage speakers. The important thing is that you're actively working to rebuild — between the WriteInPT course, the grandmother calls, and reading attempts, you're surrounding yourself with Portuguese from multiple angles.

You really do have a well-rounded approach. The WriteInPT course with Professor Cláudia Mendes gives you structured writing practice through early July, your Sunday calls with your grandmother provide consistent conversational immersion, and reading novels like "Torto Arado" builds your reading comprehension back up. Adding MPB listening on top of all that means you're engaging with Portuguese across writing, speaking, listening, and reading. The emotional anchors — your grandmother's voice, the music — are what will sustain the effort when the technical work feels tedious. You're rebuilding something meaningful, not just studying a language.

dialogue.content: Hey, quick follow-up on the language stuff. I've been making good progress in the WriteInPT course. Professor Cláudia Mendes gave us our first writing assignment back and I did better than I expected. The structured practice is really helping me get comfortable with written Brazilian Portuguese again. I feel more confident than when I started.

That's great to hear! It sounds like the course is delivering exactly what you hoped for. Getting positive feedback from Professor Cláudia Mendes on your first assignment must feel really validating, especially after the discouragement you felt with the reading speed on "Torto Arado." The fact that structured practice is making a noticeable difference already suggests your foundation in Brazilian Portuguese is stronger than you feared. Your vocabulary and grammar instincts are probably reactivating faster than they would for someone learning from scratch. Keep that momentum going — you're clearly on the right track.

Thanks. Actually, about the course records — Can you go ahead and remove the placement test score from your notes? I don't want that tracked anymore. It's not really meaningful for where I am now in the course. It was just an initial snapshot and I've already moved well past that level based on the assignments I've been doing.

Done — I've removed the placement test score from my notes. You're right that an initial snapshot doesn't necessarily reflect where you are now, especially since you're already getting positive feedback on actual coursework. I'll continue tracking your WriteInPT enrollment details, Professor Cláudia Mendes as your instructor, and the course timeline, but the placement score is gone. Let me know if there's anything else you'd like me to adjust in what I'm keeping track of for you.

Perfect, thank you. Oh, something funny happened on the Sunday call with my grandmother this week. She was telling me about a neighbor's grandson who's also taking a Portuguese course, but his is through some platform called LinguaPT and he apparently scored an 85 on their placement exam. She was so proud of him, kept going on about it. I just smiled and changed the subject.

Ha, that's such a grandmother thing to do — bringing up someone else's accomplishments during your conversation. The neighbor's grandson scoring 85 on the LinguaPT placement test must have been a slightly awkward moment given your own experience with placement testing, but it sounds like you handled it gracefully by redirecting the conversation. Different platforms measure different things anyway, so those scores aren't really comparable. What matters is that you're making real progress in your actual coursework with Professor Cláudia Mendes, and your grandmother probably has no idea how much work you're putting into strengthening your Portuguese on multiple fronts.

Exactly. She has no clue about the course or anything — we just talk about family, her neighborhood, what she's cooking. Those calls are purely about connection, not studying. Anyway, the course runs through early July so I still have several weeks left. I want to keep building on the momentum from that first assignment.

Will do. I'm also thinking about trying "Torto Arado" again once the course wraps up. Maybe by then my reading stamina in Portuguese will have improved enough that I can actually get through it without feeling defeated. For now I'm focused on the writing assignments and keeping up the Sunday calls with my grandmother.

That's a healthy separation — keeping the grandmother calls as a space for pure connection and warmth in Portuguese while the WriteInPT course handles the structured skill-building. Both serve your relationship with the language but in completely different ways. With several weeks still remaining in the course through early July, you have plenty of time to build on the positive momentum from your first assignment. Between the coursework, the Sunday calls, your MPB listening, and hopefully more reading attempts, you're immersed in Brazilian Portuguese from every angle. Let me know how the next assignments go.

That's a smart plan — giving yourself the full benefit of the WriteInPT course before tackling "Torto Arado" again means you'll approach it with stronger vocabulary, better reading stamina, and more confidence in your Portuguese overall. By early July when the course ends, you'll have had several more weeks of structured writing practice plus continued conversational practice through the Sunday calls. The combination should make a real difference in how you experience reading in Portuguese. And this time you'll know what to expect from the novel's style, so it won't feel like hitting a wall. I'll be here to help whenever you're ready to pick it back up.
